extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policymakers, judges, and students working on administrative law, presidential power, and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and explanatory framework for how presidential power over administrative policymaking depends on two necessary components—control and administrative capacity—and how variation in capacity affects rulemaking outcomes. The article uses surveys, personnel records, and statistical models to measure capacity and assess its interaction with presidential control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential control (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential control is the power to direct administrative capacity toward the President’s own policy objectives; the President must have the ability to set the agency’s policymaking agenda and direct the day-to-day activities of its leadership and career employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a necessary component of presidential power vis-à-vis administrative policymaking. The article’s survey evidence shows Presidents and their proxies exercise a great degree of control over agencies’ rulemaking agendas. However, control alone may be insufficient to secure policy outcomes in low-capacity agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative capacity (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative capacity requires a well-managed team of policymakers with expertise and experience in both the substantive policy area and the policymaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity is framed as the complement to control—without sufficient expertise, experience, and managerial quality, agencies cannot reliably implement presidential preferences. The article emphasizes empirical measurement of capacity and documents wide variation across federal agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and capacity as complementary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential power over agency policymaking has two necessary components—control and capacity—and these are complements, not substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when Presidents have significant control, low-capacity agencies are less likely to complete rulemakings. Therefore both components must be present for effective implementation; reliance on control alone is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in policymaking capacity across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: New measures of policymaking capacity show wider variation across federal agencies than is often assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding based on a survey of federal executives, more than 115 million federal personnel records, and over 5,000 rulemakings from three presidencies. Practitioners and scholars should not assume uniform capacity; evaluation of agency ability must account for this heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity predicts rulemaking completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling for presidential control and priorities, low-capacity agencies are less likely to complete their rulemakings than high-capacity agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multivariate models demonstrate this relationship; thus completion of rulemakings is offered as an outcome metric for assessing whether presidents can implement their agendas. This suggests measuring capacity is crucial for predicting policy implementation success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional markers of presidential control may be ineffective in low-capacity agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional markers of presidential control prove ineffective in low-capacity agencies, meaning standard measures of 'control' do not guarantee policy implementation when capacity is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both an empirical finding and a caution: relying on appointment power or structural changes to claim control can be misleading if the agency lacks experienced staff or managerial quality. Policymakers should consider capacity impacts when increasing direct control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between control and capacity (hiring/management effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: As presidential control increases within an agency, the agency may struggle to hire expert and experienced employees; control and capacity are in tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies an anti-pattern where strong adherence to unitary executive theory or efforts to reduce structural insulation can unintentionally erode administrative capacity. The article recommends shifting the balance toward effective management to preserve expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: managerial prerogative with oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting the President with the managerial prerogative requires increased oversight from the courts, Congress, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the tension between control and capacity, institutional checks and broader oversight are recommended to ensure managerial choices do not degrade agency capacity or frustrate implementation of congressional delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical standards and methodology transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous empirical assessment of capacity should use multiple data sources (surveys of federal executives, comprehensive personnel records, and rulemaking datasets) and disclose methodology (see Appendix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes an Appendix detailing methodology and notes human subjects review and approvals—implicit standards for reproducible and ethically reviewed empirical work in this domain.
